title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
hookLine: a census, a long walk, a full inn, and a child laid in a feeding trough
tomorrow: who's awake at 3 a.m. when good news breaks?
last: THE ONE WHO SAYS NOTHING AND STAYS.

cards: Picture the house at the holidays. Cousins on air mattresses, coats piled on a bed, an uncle asleep on the couch, a kitchen too full to turn around in. Every room is taken.
Now someone arrives late, with a baby on the way. Where do they go? Luke's answer is two words that stay with people: no room.
And the place the baby ends up is somewhere you'd smell before you see it.

teach.h: A CENSUS, A TOWN, A TROUGH.
teach.b: Luke sets it up with paperwork. Caesar Augustus orders the whole world enrolled, so Joseph goes to Bethlehem, the town of King David, with Mary, very pregnant.

Then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough.

Hay, the breath of animals, the smell of a barn: that's the first bed. Now the surprise. Luke's Greek word for inn, kataluma, is the word he uses later for the upstairs room of the Last Supper, from day two.

teach.h: KATALUMA — A GUEST ROOM, NOT A HOTEL.
teach.b: So some scholars read it as a guest room in a family house, not a hotel, with the animals brought in at night just below.
Guest room full, so the baby goes down by the troughs. And there's no innkeeper in Luke at all; the Christmas plays added him.
Catholics call this the Incarnation: God becoming flesh, a real baby who needed feeding and changing, choosing the low place, the Magnificat's lowly lifted, lived out.
Twelve centuries later, Francis of Assisi, from day seventeen, set up a real manger with a real ox and donkey at Greccio, so people could see how poor it was.
Tradition traces the Christmas crib scene to that night.

how: Catholics celebrate the birth of Jesus at Christmas, with Mass at midnight and on Christmas Day, and many families and parishes set up a nativity scene, a custom traced to Francis of Assisi at Greccio in 1223.

games.q: your parish is building a nativity display and wants every piece to match Luke. which piece makes the cut?
o: a grumpy innkeeper shutting the door.
a baby laid in the animals' feeding trough.
a hotel stable out back with a full sign.
games.why: only the trough is in Luke. there's no innkeeper, and kataluma may mean a family's guest room, not a hotel.

practice: Get up and walk to the smallest space you can reach in a minute: a closet, a pantry, a bathroom, the back seat of a car. Stand in it, and notice the smell, how close the walls are, what you can hear through them.
Luke's story starts in a space like this, and it was chosen. Before you step out, let one person come to mind who has no room today: no seat, no bed, no place at anyone's table.

wordCard.voice: No room. Two words from Luke: a full house, and a baby laid where the animals eat.

orig.note: Greek: a lodging, a guest room. the same word Luke uses for the room of the Last Supper.

carryVoice: Keep this: he chose the smallest room, with a feeding trough for a first bed. That's twenty-five.
